meta.title: Underwater Hockey: Original Formations, Tactical Sequences and Supervised Practice
meta.contentStatus: Original educational draft. Qualified underwater-hockey coaching and safety review recommended before using in a session. Not an official CMAS coaching programme.
meta.composition: Five formation studies, ten distinct tactical sequences and fourteen original practice cards. Diagrams and drills were composed for this atlas rather than copied from external diagrams or manuals.

board.coordinateSystem: Normalized Cartesian-like board coordinates: x increases left to right from 0 to 100; y increases top to bottom from 0 to 100.
board.poolScale: Conceptual teaching board, not to scale. Positions, paths, apparent distances, goal icon width and spacing are not official pool requirements or guaranteed playable distances.
board.orientation: Use the same orientation in every sequence; do not silently flip the board during a turnover. Changing possession changes the carrier, not the team attack directions.

legend.meaning: Six Team A role markers. Letters/labels remain visible so colour is not the only identifier.
Selected Team B opponents relevant to the illustrated problem; not a complete opposition lineup.
Puck; draw a distinct small labelled disc. carrierId is schematic possession, not literal puck balance on a stick.
Player movement without the puck: action kind move.
Player and puck move together along the floor: action kind carry. This never means lifting and carrying a balanced puck.
Puck pass: action kind pass. Direction is start to end; default trajectory is a controlled floor-level pass, with no prescribed lift.
Player currently at the surface. That player is unavailable as an immediate underwater receiver in this illustrated frame.

legend.symbol: Unfilled role marker with R badge
legend.meaning: Reference-only formation role; no claim about current depth or availability.
Hold a reference position for the board discussion; never an instruction to hold breath or delay surfacing.

availabilityValues.available: A player currently represented as able to participate in this decision snapshot; no duration or dive schedule is implied.
availabilityValues.surface: Currently at the surface; the board must not use this player as an immediate underwater receiving target.

board.timing: No seconds, swim speeds, breath-hold durations or dive intervals are encoded. Each frame is a decision snapshot. Stop/play controls are for board animation only and must not become in-water pace commands.
board.pathInterpretation: Ordered polylines are illustrative routes. They do not depict bodies, fins, legal clearance distances or tackle mechanics. A puck marker shares its carrier coordinate for readable state bookkeeping; do not interpret that co-location as literal technique.
board.renderingSafety: Keep the availability legend and free-surfacing note visible. Do not style surface players as failed or penalized. Do not award points for completing a sequence without surfacing.
board.accessibility: Render each sequence and step textAlternative beside or as an accessible alternative to the board; preserve keyboard next/previous controls, readable actor labels, non-colour line styles and a reduced-motion/manual-step option.

schemaGuide.formations: Each has six roleResponsibilities linked by actorId to referenceState.players, explanatory arrays, sourceIds and a textAlternative.
schemaGuide.sequences: Each has initialState plus ordered steps. Every step includes a complete resulting state, allowing Previous/Reset without reversing animation math.
schemaGuide.state: players is the complete displayed actor list with id, team, label, role, position{x,y}, availability. puck has position{x,y}, carrierId (actor ID or null).
schemaGuide.actions: Each step action has an order, actorId, kind, path of at least two {x,y} points and a note. Apply actions in order. Path begins at the preceding state or preceding action endpoint. Intermediate polyline points are optional.

actionKinds.move: Move actor only; puck does not move.
actionKinds.carry: Move actor and its controlled puck together.
actionKinds.pass: Move puck only from actor to targetActorId; objectId is puck; receiving actor stays at its current coordinate.
actionKinds.surface: Change actor availability to surface; repeated x/y point depicts no horizontal path.
actionKinds.available: Change actor availability to available only when the real player is ready; not used as a scheduled dive instruction.
actionKinds.recover: Assumed legal change of possession for a teaching scenario, with former carrier recorded; not a technical tackle animation.
actionKinds.hold: No state change; highlights the actor’s current role.

schemaGuide.branches: Optional non-animated alternatives to a decision point; illustrated=true marks the branch drawn in the main steps. Other alternatives must not be presented as prevalidated coordinate paths.
schemaGuide.drills: Detailed standalone cards with people, equipment, setup, procedure, resetAndRotation, adaptations, coachObservations, debriefQuestions, safety and contextual sourceIds.
schemaGuide.sourceIds: Resolve within this file’s sources for a self-contained citation registry. Links supply background and applicable rules; no source is claimed to endorse an original play.

editorialLimits: These are options to discuss and adapt, not universal prescriptions, proven optimal tactics or guaranteed scoring patterns.
Role names vary across clubs and countries; the labels here are declared for consistency within the board.
Five formation diagrams contain exactly six Team A players. Partial opponent diagrams deliberately omit irrelevant markers and must disclose that omission.
No copied diagrams, proprietary drills, photographs, video files or rulebook pages are included. No permission to mirror the linked sources is implied.
No official restart, penalty-shot, substitution-area or pool-measurement procedure is illustrated. Consult applicable current rules for those requirements.
A tactic may be interrupted at any point by surfacing, a changed opponent position or an unsafe/closed route.

safety.requiredContext: In-water use requires a properly supervised underwater-hockey session, competent coaching, designated rescue cover and the venue’s emergency plan. A partner or a diagram alone does not establish adequate supervision.
nonNegotiables: Never practise underwater breath holding alone; do not hyperventilate, run maximum-hold or distance challenges, or ask anyone to ignore the urge to breathe.
Players surface whenever they need, including in the middle of a pass pattern. Give unobstructed routes to the surface and use suitable recovery under the session’s safety plan.
End a teaching repetition for surfacing, equipment trouble, lost control, congestion or the agreed stop signal. Resume only after the coach’s safe reset and readiness check.
Keep stick and puck play controlled, avoid unsafe lifted trajectories, and do not use off-puck screens, pushing, pulling, holding or active obstruction.
Use the club’s medical, safeguarding, equipment and incident procedures; these cards provide no individual medical clearance or rescue certification.
safety.trainingFocus: Measure quality of decisions, control and support. Do not measure success by submersion duration, breath-hold capacity, forced repetitions or suppressing surfacing.

concepts.title: Read formation numbers front to back
concepts.body: The first number describes the most attacking reference line; the last describes the deepest. On this board Team A attacks upward. A role can move into another layer as play changes, so the numbers describe a shared starting language rather than fixed coordinates.

concepts.title: Support and cover answer different questions
concepts.body: With the puck, ask who can receive and improve the next decision. Without it, ask who can contest the live puck and who can respond after that contest. One person may switch between these jobs within a phase. Naming the job is more useful than demanding that a player return to an arbitrary dot.

concepts.title: The puck side can change in one pass
concepts.body: Puck-side means the side of the current puck; far-side means the other side. Those descriptions are relative to play, not permanent player identities. After a switch, old puck-side players may become far-side support. Reassess the available routes rather than simply mirroring every movement.

concepts.title: A role is not the same as an available receiver
concepts.body: An advanced player at the surface is still part of the team but is not an immediate underwater pass target. Read the actual people and choose a shorter option when needed. No tactical handover asks someone to delay surfacing or dive before ready. The board’s surface badge makes this visible.

concepts.title: Create passing routes without blocking opponents
concepts.body: A teammate can move into clear space to become a receiver. That does not authorise screening, grabbing, pushing or using the free arm to deny an opponent access. Interpret every arrow as a legal movement option subject to the current rules and the actual positions of everyone nearby.

concepts.title: Practise the cue as well as the pattern
concepts.body: Start with one clear problem, ask what the defender changes, and compare two plausible responses. If the expected lane disappears, a different choice or a safe reset can be the right outcome. A completed drawn pattern is weak evidence of learning unless the players can explain when it would help.

coachGuide.title: Use a sequence as a question
procedure: Begin on a dry board. Name the attack direction, the current carrier and the players marked at the surface.
Show only the initial frame. Ask for two possible next actions and which visible cue would favour each.
Step through the example manually. Keep opponent movements visible and treat each shown route as conditional.
Move an opponent or mark a receiver at the surface. Ask what changes before replaying.
For supervised pool use, select a suitable drill card, agree the stop/reset plan, confirm protective equipment and rescue arrangements, and scale the area to the group.
Coach one observable, then stop for recovery and a surface debrief. Increase only one decision constraint at a time; never use longer submersion as the progression.
discussionPrompts: What does the carrier know here?
What can the opponent do to remove that option?
Who covers if this attempt fails?
What changes if a player surfaces?
coachGuide.sessionPlanning: Choose a small number of ideas appropriate to the session rather than trying to complete this library. The cards intentionally specify resets and role rotations rather than a universal duration, underwater distance or breath-hold target.

formations.status: Established community notation; original teaching interpretation
formations.summary: Two reference lines make support and cover easy to discuss: three forward roles and three back roles.
formations.explanation: Start by agreeing what each line contributes around the puck. The front group offers attacking options; the back group connects possession and provides depth if play reverses. The lines need not remain straight or equally spaced. Near a wall, the puck-side players can work closer together while the far side stays useful rather than simply copying the same distance from the wall. A six-dot drawing describes the team’s responsibilities over a phase of play. It does not show six people staying on the bottom. When someone surfaces, the available players read the gap and simplify the next decision.

roleResponsibilities.responsibility: Offer a left-side outlet, then find a reachable position after releasing the puck.
Connect the attacking options; change depth when the central lane is crowded.
Offer a right-side outlet and remain aware of a switch toward the far side.
Connect behind a left-side attack and be ready to defend a lost puck.
Keep a useful central covering position instead of joining every nearby contest.
Connect behind a right-side attack and watch the space away from the puck.

inPossession: Give the carrier at least one short playable option rather than three distant targets.
Let one forward come closer if both forward passes are closed.
A back can advance with space if another available player recognises the covering job.
outOfPossession: Separate the player challenging the puck from players protecting the next route.
If the puck changes sides, transfer puck-side responsibility instead of dragging the whole team into one cluster.
onTurnover: After losing it, identify the immediate threat and the route toward your own goal.
After winning it, find an available teammate before expecting the front line to race away.
tradeoffs: Simple line vocabulary can help a new team discuss responsibilities.
Two flat lines can create a large unplayable gap; stagger individuals rather than worshipping the shape.
Three players up front are wasted if all ask for the same pass.
discussionQuestions: Which forward could come closer without duplicating the carrier?
What cover remains if the nearest back advances?

formations.status: Established community notation; original teaching interpretation
formations.summary: A paired front line and three-player connecting line leave one named deep covering role.
formations.explanation: Use this shape to discuss how a middle line can connect two advanced options while preserving someone behind the engagement. The deep player is a team role, not a goalkeeper tied to the goal. If that player becomes the puck carrier, another available teammate must notice what changed. The forward pair can be staggered rather than shoulder to shoulder: one may offer the immediate pass while the other reads the next space. Near a wall, the far midfielder must decide whether a switch is genuinely reachable or whether moving closer is more useful.

roleResponsibilities.responsibility: Offer a left-biased attacking option and return toward play if isolated.
Offer a second attacking option at a different angle or depth.
Connect the left channel with central support.
Offer a short linking option and recognise when deeper cover needs replacing.
Keep a useful right-side connection without abandoning the rest of the team.
Observe behind the middle line; engage when useful with another player recognising the covering task.

inPossession: Use the middle line to shorten a pass rather than sending a blind puck toward the forwards.
After a pass toward a side, replace the support angle behind the new carrier.
outOfPossession: Keep central recovery space visible to the middle group.
The deep back should not be the only person reacting to a turnover.
onTurnover: If the deep back engages, an available midfielder can move into the deeper role.
The forward nearest a loose puck can help reconnect; nominal role names do not forbid recovery.
tradeoffs: The middle group gives several possible connections across the pool.
A single deep role can become isolated if the middle group advances together.
Role handovers matter more than a rigid three-line picture.
coachCues: The deep role still belongs to somebody
discussionQuestions: Who covers if the deep back receives and advances?
Which midfielder is actually reachable from the wall?

formations.status: Original teaching interpretation of a community formation label; no universal role specification claimed
formations.summary: Three pairs offer a clear way to examine depth, cross-pool connection and paired covering roles.
formations.explanation: This is an original teaching interpretation of a six-player 2–2–2 shape. Read it as three layers of responsibility, not six rails to follow. A pair can be offset diagonally so its players do not offer the identical option. The middle pair often has an important choice: support the current side or stay available for the next connection. Neither decision is automatically correct. If the pool looks divided into two disconnected three-player columns, bring a connecting player inward or backward before attempting a long forced pass. Coaches should adapt the role names and spacing to the players they actually have.

roleResponsibilities.responsibility: Offer a left attacking route while staying within the team’s usable range.
Offer a different front-line route, including a short return option when needed.
Link the puck side to the next layer and notice central space.
Provide a second linking angle rather than matching the other midfielder exactly.
Cover behind the left-biased engagement and exchange jobs with the other back as play shifts.
Cover behind the right-biased engagement and avoid committing to the same contest as the other back.

inPossession: Seek small diagonals between layers rather than only straight-ahead passes.
Change one partner’s depth if a defender can close both options from the same position.
outOfPossession: One player can contest while a partner stays able to respond to the next puck movement.
Watch the central channel if both members of a pair are drawn toward separate walls.
onTurnover: Reform useful links around the puck before trying to restore perfectly symmetrical pairs.
A midfield player may temporarily be the deepest available cover.
tradeoffs: Paired roles make contrasting decisions easy to rehearse on a board.
Two separated columns can leave the middle unconnected.
The extra line can create too much distance between roles if spacing is copied literally.
discussionQuestions: Which two players are offering the same lane?
Would a shorter diagonal connect the layers?

formations.status: Established community notation; original teaching interpretation
formations.summary: One advanced role, three connecting roles and two backs invite discussion about reachability and balanced support.
formations.explanation: The single forward is useful only if the rest of the team can connect with that player. The midfield can move the puck sideways or recycle it to change the available lane, and an available midfielder can become the next attacking receiver. Two named backs offer a natural conversation about who contests and who stays able to answer the next threat. They do not guarantee cover if both chase the same puck. This board uses a modestly staggered middle line as a teaching choice; clubs may interpret the same formation quite differently.

roleResponsibilities.responsibility: Offer an advanced option without becoming disconnected from the puck.
Connect the left side, choosing whether to support behind or move into a new receiving lane.
Provide a central link and help the team recognise changes in possession.
Connect the right side and remain available when play switches.
Read whether to contest or protect the next threat with the other back.
Complement the other back rather than duplicate the same engagement.

inPossession: Let a short sideways or backward pass improve the next picture.
A midfielder may become a second advanced option when space and available cover permit.
outOfPossession: Watch the area around the midfield as well as the immediate puck carrier.
Stagger the backs’ decisions so they do not both disappear into one contest.
onTurnover: The nearest available midfield player may become immediate cover.
A regained puck does not have to go straight to the lone forward.
tradeoffs: Three connecting roles offer several ways to reorganise possession.
The lone forward can be isolated if the middle group stays too deep.
Both backs chasing one contest removes the benefit of naming a pair.
discussionQuestions: Can the forward receive under control from here?
If this back engages, which threat can the other still answer?

formations.status: Original comparative coaching shape; not presented as a federation-endorsed system
formations.summary: Three advanced roles with two connectors and one deep role make an instructive attacking-versus-cover comparison.
formations.explanation: Treat this shape as a board experiment for an experienced coach, not a recommendation for every team. The front group has several possible receiving lanes, but those options matter only while the two midfielders can connect them to the puck. A lone deep role raises a useful question: who helps when the puck is lost or when that player surfaces? The practical answer may be to lower one forward, move a midfielder back, or abandon the drawn shape for the current phase. Comparing this picture with 3–3 can reveal whether an extra apparent attacking layer adds useful options or simply separates the team.

roleResponsibilities.responsibility: Offer an attacking lane to the left and recover toward play when the connection disappears.
Change depth to become a linking receiver if both midfielders are pressured.
Offer an attacking lane to the right without waiting beyond a realistic pass.
Connect the left half and recognise when covering depth is absent.
Connect the right half and share responsibility for rebuilding after a loss.
Hold a useful deeper reference position; seek help rather than being expected to solve every counterattack.

inPossession: Choose one or two genuinely reachable front options instead of treating all three as a required pass.
An advanced player can come back toward the midfield to restore connection.
outOfPossession: Name the second covering player before committing another person forward.
As pressure increases, temporarily using fewer advanced roles can preserve a playable team.
onTurnover: Nearest pressure and deeper recovery are separate jobs.
A midfielder can recover centrally while the nearest forward reconnects behind the puck.
tradeoffs: Several advanced lanes can expose whether the opposition is stretched.
The linking pair may be outnumbered or bypassed.
One nominal deep role increases the importance of availability and role changes.
coachCues: Recover the centre first when that is the live threat
discussionQuestions: Does the third advanced player add a usable option?
Which temporary role swap makes a lost puck less dangerous?

sequences.title: Recycle into a new passing lane
sequences.purpose: Use a short backward connection to change the angle of the next forward pass.
sequences.scenario: A1 has the puck in the left half. B1 closes the direct forward route and B2 narrows the inside lane. A4 can become a reachable trailing option. A3 and A6 are currently at the surface.
sequences.attackDirection: A toward y=0; B toward y=100
recognitionCues: The carrier’s forward lane is crowded.
A trailing teammate is available with a clear short pass.
counterplay: A defender can follow the trailing receiver; the recycle only helps if the new picture improves.
An opponent can anticipate the second pass, so reassess after the first.
tradeoffs: The team gives up some territory to preserve a usable next action.
Recycling too far or toward a recovering player can disconnect possession.

actions.note: Make the short return pass into A4’s usable reach.

sequences.takeaway: A backward pass can create progress when it changes the next available angle. It is a decision tool, not a required extra pass.
debriefQuestions: What made the original forward pass unattractive?
Which movement changed the second passing lane?

sequences.title: Leave the wall through trailing support
sequences.purpose: Move out of a crowded wall pocket through a controlled backward-diagonal release.
sequences.scenario: A3 carries near the left boundary. B1 is ahead and B2 is inside, making a direct push up the wall unattractive. A4 is the potential trailing connector; A2 and A5 are at the surface.
sequences.attackDirection: A toward y=0; B toward y=100
recognitionCues: Both the wall-forward route and the immediate inside route are crowded.
A clear route exists backward and away from the barrier.
counterplay: An opponent may drop into the trailing pass; there is no guaranteed exit.

drills.title: Controlled approach, two exits
drills.purpose: Keep the puck playable while changing direction, then release it to a visible receiver without chasing speed.

people.supervision: Qualified UWH supervisor and designated rescue cover, with a pool emergency plan. Peer observers never replace safety cover.

equipment: Pool-approved UWH protective kit and sticks
drills.setup: Mark two wide gates in a roughly 3-by-3-metre area. Receiver waits beyond one gate, clear of its approach. Adapt spacing to the players.
procedure: At the surface, identify the occupied gate and agree one controlled carry followed by one pass.
When ready, the carrier approaches with small touches, keeping the puck within a comfortable playing reach.
Turn toward the receiver's gate without cutting across the receiver; look up before passing along the floor.
End after the receiver controls the puck, after a lost puck, or whenever either player surfaces. Do not add a return leg.
drills.resetAndRotation: Recover at the surface, exchange one observation, then swap roles. Alternate gates between separate attempts; the coach resets the puck when safe.

adaptations.easier: Use one gate and a stationary receiver nearer the starting position.
adaptations.harder: Change the receiver's gate before each attempt; add a second possible approach angle, not a longer underwater route.

coachObservations: Touches remain recoverable rather than stretching into a chase
The final look precedes the pass
debriefQuestions: Which touch made the turn easier?
Could the receiver predict where the puck would arrive?

drills.title: Pause, predict, check
drills.purpose: Practise evidence-based tactical observation and choose one testable coaching adjustment without judging unseen intentions.

roles: One rotating note-taker; roles may overlap
people.supervision: A coach or facilitator runs this classroom activity; no in-water participation is included.

equipment: Licensed or club-authorised short match clip, or original storyboard

procedure: Pause before a pass or turnover. Identify carrier, visible options and important areas outside the camera view.

Agree one small adjustment to test in a later supervised drill and one observable sign that it helped.

adaptations.easier: Use a labelled still image or an original three-player storyboard.
adaptations.harder: Compare two similar situations with different outcomes and identify what the camera cannot establish.

Which action would we test, and what evidence could change our view?
